course_name: Natural language processing in Health and Social Care
description: Explore the fundamentals of Natural Language Processing (NLP), a key AI branch focused on interpreting and analysing human language. This course highlights NLP’s growing role in health and social care, where vast text data, from electronic health records to medical literature and social media, offers rich insights. Learn technical skills with cutting-edge NLP tools and develop a critical understanding of the ethical and social implications of handling text data. The course combines theory and practice to prepare you for the rapidly evolving field of NLP in health and social care. Theory videos is presented by Dr Arlene Casey with a decade of experience in analysing text in healthcare, while practice exercises in R will take you from separating text into tokens, all the way to processing hundreds of written documents.

notes: This course will teach basic statistical techniques for describing data and examining relationships between data (correlation, differences between groups, etc.). If you took the Intro to stats course and struggled a bit and would like to have another run-through of the content, with slightly more R focus, then taking the Data Analysis course is a good idea. If you are feeling (or by the end of the course do feel) really confident and wants to progress with stats, then Statistical Modelling is a good choice.

course_name: Data visualisation: Knowledge transfer
description: This course will introduce you to data visualisation as a challenging and creative activity. Nurturing your critical thinking skills and capacity to ‘think outside the square’, instead of jumping straight to coding solutions, you will focus on developing new ways of seeing and conceptualising data. You will be introduced to data visualisation theory and challenged to put theory into practice as you think, doodle and sketch data. This course develops critical thinking skills, encourages engagement with real-world problems and comes with a promise that once completed you will never look at a bar chart, a scatter plot or a heat map the same way again. No programming will be used on this course. Workshops and assessment will be delivered by discussing and (crudely) drawing variants of data visualisations.
notes: There is NO PROGRAMMING in this course

course_name: Foundations of Software Development in Health and Social Care (Python 1)

notes: This is an introductory course in Python programming - it should be taken by students who are absolute beginners to Python and programming practices, and it will provide a solid foundation to using programming to solve issues in health and social care.

course_name: Introduction to Databases & Information Systems

course_name: AI for care in the digital age
description: As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into health and social care services, understanding its implications is more important than ever. Developing and using AI tools requires more than an understanding of algorithms and technology, though it is very important. Also, it involves navigating complex issues related to, for example, data quality, ethics, governance, interoperability, and stakeholder engagement. This course will equip you with the knowledge and critical thinking skills needed to evaluate, implement, and influence the responsible use of AI within your organisation or service. Through real-world examples, case studies, and expert insights, you will analyse challenges and opportunities across the AI lifecycle and develop eventually the confidence to contribute to informed decision-making in the digital age.

course_name: Foundations of Machine Learning in HSC
description: This course introduces the foundations of machine learning through practical examples from health and social care. Rather than treating algorithms as a purely technical topic, it considers how machine learning works in clinical and social care settings, including its limitations and implications for decisions about people. You will develop an understanding of the statistical reasoning behind supervised and unsupervised learning, build and compare regression and classification models, and assess model performance through case studies and weekly pair-programming tutorial. The course also considers the ethics of using machine learning in health and social care, including critical consideration of the trade-offs involved in choosing different models. By the end of the course, you will have experience building and evaluating machine learning models and a clearer understanding of how they can be used in health and social care.
notes: This course has pre-requirements around statistics AND Python programming

course_name: Applied research design for data science in Health and Social Care
description: This course develops the practical skills needed to create a clear, robust and responsible research proposal. You will move from a broad research topic to focused aims and objectives, drafting effective background and methods sections. You will explore qualitative and mixed-methods approaches and health and social care data sources. The course introduces open research, copyright, licensing, plagiarism, referencing and journal publishing. You will be introduced to managing research data, including FAIR principles, secure storage, Trusted Research Environments, data management plans, documentation, data dictionaries and cleaning spreadsheets. You will also learn about open research, version control and GitHub repositories. Through data visualisation, lay summaries and audience-focused communication, you will develop the skills to share research transparently, responsibly and effectively in varied contexts. This course prepares you for your dissertation year and wider research activities.

Foundations of research design for data science in Health and Social Care (Digital)
description: This course equips you with the knowledge and skills to plan, evaluate and communicate high-quality research. You will explore research principles, ethics, public engagement, protocols, research questions and literature searching, including reference management and review methods. The course introduces quantitative and epidemiological concepts, including causation, bias, confounding, chance and disease frequency, alongside choosing appropriate observational and interventional study designs. You will develop critical-appraisal skills for observational and interventional studies, systematic reviews, meta-analyses and machine-learning research, using reporting standards and appraisal tools. Live discussions and practical activities support you to narrow a topic, refine a research question, conduct a literature review and consider ethical issues for a project. You will also learn about patient and public involvement, and writing lay summaries. This course prepares you for your dissertation year and wider research activities.
